sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Huángdì** (*huangdi*) ​— The ‌Yellow Emperor ‌· Lord ​of the ​Center — ​belongs to the ​Chinese tradition, ​where it ‌is catalogued ​under the ​domain "Yellow ‌Emperor, Ancestor". ​The name means ‌"Yellow emperor"[^1].

​**Huángdì** — ‌the Yellow ​Emperor, Xuānyuán ​of the ​Bear clan — ​is the ​founding ancestor ‌the Chinese ​tradition gave ‌itself: **the ​sovereign who won ‌the land ​at Banquan ‌and Zhuolu, ​ordered the ‌calendar and ​the script, and ​rode a ‌yellow dragon ‌up to ‌Heaven** when ​his work ​was done. ‌A culture-hero of ​the late ​Warring States ‌imagination, he ​became what ​the Shiji ‌made him: the ​first of ‌the Five ​Emperors, ancestor ​of all ​who call ​themselves children of ‌Yán and ‌Huáng.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores the ‌name as ​**Huángdì** and ​serves its ‌temple at [huángdì.com](https://xn--hungd-yqa4f.com). ‌The restoration ‌preserves at ‌least one ​distinctive feature ‌— a ​diacritic or a ​distinctive letter ​— that ‌the ASCII ​form loses, ​and exactly ​one historically valid ‌Unicode restoration ​exists, which ​places the ​name in ‌Tier 1. ​The plain ASCII ‌form *huangdi* ​survives as ‌a modern ​convenience imposed ‌by the ‌early domain-name ​system; the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Chinese characters ​as ​**黄帝**. Etymologically ​it means ​"Yellow emperor"[^1].

​The ‌ASCII form ​*huangdi* survives ​only because ‌the ​early domain-name ‌system could ​not carry ‌diacritics; ​it is ​a technological ​compromise, not ​an ​ancient spelling. ‌The Unicode ​restoration **Huángdì** ‌recovers ​the stress ‌accent of ​the original ‌directly ​in the ‌address bar. ​The restoration ​preserves ‌at least ‌one distinctive ‌feature — ​a ​diacritic or ‌a distinctive ​letter — ​that ‌the ASCII ​form loses, ​and exactly ‌one ​historically valid ‌Unicode restoration ​exists, which ​places ​the name ​in Tier ‌1.

The ‌letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

‌- **h** ​→ **H** ​— ‌Same, capitalized
‌- **u** ‌→ **u** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**a** → ​**á** — ​Stress ​on a
‌- **n** ​→ **n** ​— ​Same
- ‌**g** → ​**g** — ​Same
​- **d** ‌→ **d** ​— Same
‌- ​**i** → ‌**ì** — ​Stress on ‌i

‌The project ​holds the ​domain **huángdì.com** ​(xn--hungd-yqa4f.com) ​as the ‌canonical home ‌of this ​name[^2].

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of the ‌name is **/xua˧˥ŋ. ti˥˩/** ‌— Modern Standard ​Mandarin (Pinyin).[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

- ​**Huáng** — The ​pinyin h is the ​velar fricative [x] ‌— the 'ch' ​of Scottish 'loch', ​not an English h; ‌the diphthong glides ​[u→a] into the ‌velar nasal [ŋ], ​'ng' as in 'sing', ‌all on the ​second tone: a ​rising glide, ˧˥.
​- **Dì** — ​Voiceless unaspirated [t] — ​the 't' of ‌'stay' — on ​high front [i]; ‌the fourth tone falls ​hard through the ‌register, ˥˩, like ​a door closing: ‌apt for 帝, ​'sovereign, thearch.'

For the ‌modern speaker, the ​closest approximation is: ​'HWAHNG-dee' — 'hwang' ‌rising as though the ‌syllable itself were ‌climbing, 'dee' dropping ​decisively: rise, then ​fall.

Kindred and historical ‌forms of the ​name:

- **Traditional** ​— 黃帝 Huángdì ‌— 黃 'yellow' ​+ 帝 'sovereign'; not ​皇帝 huángdì 'emperor,' ‌a modern homophone, ​a different word.
‌- **Personal name** — ​軒轅 Xuānyuán, 'Chariot-Axle' ​— the name ​the Shiji gives ​him, later a ‌byword for the Yellow ‌Emperor.
- **Clan ​name** — 有熊氏 ‌Yǒuxióng shì, the ​Bear clan of which ​he was born ‌head; the Shiji ‌also gives him ‌the surname 公孫 Gōngsūn.
‌- **Paired ancestor** ​— 炎帝 Yándì, ‌the Flame Emperor ​— his defeated ​rival at Banquan, afterward ​his twin in ‌炎黃子孫, 'descendants of ​Yán and Huáng.' ​A pair, never one ​figure.

Huángdì is ‌Tier 1 because ​tone is lexical: ​the acute á ​and the grave ì ‌carry the second ​and fourth citation ‌tones, and in ​Mandarin tone is meaning ‌— mā 'mother,' ​má 'hemp,' mǎ ‌'horse,' mà 'scold.' ‌The plain ASCII 'huangdi' ​flattens both contours ​to silence. (And ​黃帝 'Yellow Emperor' ​and 皇帝 'emperor' ‌romanize identically — only ‌the characters keep ​them apart.)

sources.citation: Sima Qian, Shiji 1, “Basic Annals of the Five Emperors” (Wudi benji).

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Huángdì** — ​the Yellow ‌Emperor, Xuānyuán of ‌the Bear clan ​— is ​the founding ancestor ​the Chinese tradition ​gave itself: ​**the sovereign who ‌won the ​land at Banquan ​and Zhuolu, ordered ‌the calendar ​and the script, ‌and rode a ​yellow dragon ‌up to Heaven** ​when his ​work was done. ​A culture-hero of ​the late ​Warring States imagination, ‌he became what ​the Shiji ‌made him: the ​first of ‌the Five Emperors, ​ancestor of all ‌who call ​themselves children of ‌Yán and Huáng.[^1]

​### The ​Founder at Arms

‌Three victories ‌at Banquan over ‌the Flame Emperor ​Yándì, then ​the great battle ‌at Zhuolu where ​Chīyóu fell ​— the two ‌wars by ​which the Shiji ​says the realm ‌was first ​united (Shiji 1).

‌### First Ancestor

​炎黃子孫 yánhuáng ​zǐsūn, 'descendants of ​Yán and ​Huáng' — the ‌name a fifth ‌of humanity ​calls itself; his ‌tomb at Qiaoshan ​is honored ​as the ancestral ‌root of ‌the entire people.

‌### Giver of ‌the Arts

​Writing by his ‌scribe Cāng Jié, ​the sixty-year ​cycle by Dà ​Náo, the ‌twelve pitch-pipes by ​Líng Lún, silk ​by his ​wife Léi Zǔ, ‌medicine in his ​dialogues with ​Qí Bó — ​civilization chartered ‌in one reign.

​### The Model ‌of Rule

​The golden-age sovereign: ‌'he made the ​officials by ‌the clouds and ‌the hosts ​by the signs' ​— the template ​every dynasty ​measured itself against, ‌the face on ‌the Huáng-Lǎo ​school's banner.

sources.citation: Sima Qian, Shiji 28, “Treatise on the Feng and Shan Sacrifices” (the ascent at Jingshan).

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography ​associated with Huángdì ‌concentrates in a small ‌set of recurring ​attributes, each a ​compressed statement about the ​name:[^1]

- **The ​Yellow Dragon** — ​At the end of ‌his reign a ​dragon descended to ​carry him to Heaven ‌(Shiji 28) — ​the animal that ‌is China itself, ​come to fetch the ‌man who made ​it; 'descendants of ​the dragon' is the ​people's other name.
​- **The color ​yellow and the Center** ‌— In five-phase ​cosmology yellow belongs ‌to the Earth phase ​and the center ‌of space — ​the axis he ‌holds among the Five ​Emperors; dynasties claimed ‌imperial yellow as ​his inheritance.
- **The ​clouds as emblem** ‌— The Shiji ‌says he 'took the ‌clouds as his ​emblem and named ​his officers from the ‌clouds' — Heaven's ​weather turned into ​a ministry, the ‌first charter of bureaucracy.
​- **The south-pointing ​chariot** — Later ‌tradition credits him with ​the zhǐnánchē, the ‌compass cart said ​to have led his ​army out of ​the fog Chīyóu ​raised at Zhuolu ‌— a magnetic legend, ‌whatever its date.
​- **Bears, tigers, ‌and the war-beasts** — ​For Zhuolu he ​'tamed bears, brown ‌bears, leopards, and tigers' ‌to fight for ‌him (Shiji 1) ‌— the culture-hero as ​master of the ‌wild; his clan ​name is the ​Bear (Yǒuxióng).
- **The ​precious tripod** — ‌He 'obtained the ​precious tripod and calculated ​the sun with ​counting-rods' (Shiji 1), ‌and cast a great ​cauldron from Shoushan ​copper (Shiji 28) ​— the dǐng as ‌emblem of legitimate ​rule, carried on ‌by the nine ​tripods of Yǔ.
- ‌**Mount Qiao (橋山 ​Qiáoshān)** — His ‌tomb in Huangling County, ‌Shaanxi — the ​First Tomb Under ​Heaven — said to ​hold not his ​body, snatched up ‌by the dragon, but ‌his bow, cap, ​and clothes.

sources.citation: Sima Qian, Shiji 1, “Basic Annals of the Five Emperors” (Wudi benji).

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The Yellow Emperor is the archaeologist's ​dream of a beginning: warlord, inventor, lawgiver, and immortal in ‌one. Sīmǎ Qiān's *Shǐjì* (ch. 1) gives him his biography; ‌the *Zhuāngzǐ* gives him his soul. Between the two stands ​the mythic sovereign — **victorious at Banquan and Zhuolu, ordering ​all the arts of life, and refusing to die in ​the ordinary way**.[^1]

### Xuānyuán of the Bear Clan (The ​Origins)

“The Yellow Emperor was a son of Shǎodiǎn, surnamed ​Gōngsūn, and his name was Xuānyuán.” So the *Shiji* opens ‌the first reign of Chinese history (ch. 1): born head ​of the Yǒuxióng, the Bear clan, praised in the formula of ​sage-birth legend — “born divine, he spoke early, and as ‌an infant was quick-witted” — and handed an army, not ​a cradle. Modern scholarship reads the story plainly: not an ‌excavable biography but a Warring States and Han construction, its ​earliest layers barely older than the fourth century BCE. The ‌tradition never asked to be believed as chronicle, only honored ​as charter.[^2]

### Banquan and Zhuolu (The Two Wars)

The ​founding required two victories. First, three battles at Banquan, after ​which “the hosts of the world gave allegiance to him ​where the Flame Emperor was concerned” (*Shiji* 1): Yándì, defeated, became ​not an enemy but the first subject — and, in ‌time, the twin ancestor beside him. Then the great battle: ​Chīyóu of the Jiǔlí raised a fog over the field ‌at Zhuolu, and the army lost its way — later ​tradition answered with the south-pointing chariot that always faced south, ‌however the carriage turned. The *Shiji* compresses the war into ​one sentence of terrible calm: he “waged battle with Chīyóu ‌at Zhuolu and captured and killed him.” Banquan made him ​sovereign of the willing; Zhuolu made him sovereign of the wild.

‌### The Charter of Civilization (The Ordering)

What the *Shiji* ​celebrates most is not conquest but administration — a single ​reign made to carry the list of inventions. “He took ‌the clouds as his emblem and named his officers from ‌the clouds” — the first bureaucracy. He obtained the precious ‌tripod and “calculated the sun with counting-rods”; his chronologer Dà ​Náo fixed the sixty-year cycle of stems and branches that ​still names traditional years. His music-master Líng Lún tuned the ‌twelve pitch-pipes in the valley of Xiédù; his wife Léi ​Zǔ taught the rearing of silkworms, and silk clothed an empire. ​His historian Cāng Jié invented writing — and the *Huáinánzǐ* ‌attaches to the deed one of the most haunting sentences ​in Chinese myth: “when Cāng Jié invented writing, grain rained ​from Heaven and the ghosts wailed at night.” The *Shiji*'s ‌list is the charter every guild of inventors shared.

### ​The Dragon at Jīngshān (The Ascent)

No hero of this ‌size is allowed an ordinary death. Tradition credits him with ​a century of rule; then, the *Shiji* says (ch. 28), ​he cast a great cauldron from Shǒushān copper beneath Mount ​Jīng — and when it was finished, a dragon descended, beard ​trailing low, to carry him up. He mounted with seventy ‌of his officers and households; those who could not climb ‌seized his bow and his robe, and the dragon rose ​anyway. The bow and clothes they buried at Mount Qiao ‌— which, the *Shiji* explains, is why the tomb on ​Qiaoshan stands though no body lies in it. The myth ​is the hinge of his cult: a sovereign who ascends ‌is a sovereign who watches. Every dynasty that offered at ‌his tomb was filing a report with the founder.

### ‌Guǎngchéngzǐ of Mount Kōngtóng (Zhuangzi 11) (The Philosopher's Emperor)

The *Zhuāngzǐ* ‌keeps a second, older Yellow Emperor — not the inventor ​of everything but the man who had to be unmade. ‌Desiring to govern all under Heaven well, Xuānyuán went up ​Mount Kōngtóng to ask Guǎngchéngzǐ about the essence of the ​great Way. The first interview failed: “you govern all under ​Heaven, and see that the clouds do not gather before ‌they should rain, the trees shed their leaves before they ​turn yellow, the sun and moon give light more and ​more dimly — a mind like yours is unfit to speak ​of the great Way.” The Emperor went away, gave up ‌the throne, built a solitary hut, and fasted from inquiry ​for three months. When he returned, Guǎngchéngzǐ taught him: keep ​the essence of your complete being, guard the One, live ​twelve hundred years without decline. The story is the Daoist ‌canon at its most subversive: the sovereign must shed sovereignty ​to find what sovereignty is for — the maker of ‌the state taught by the man who refused it.

### ​Xuānyuán and the Dark Pearl (Zhuangzi 12) (The Lost Pearl)

‌In another Zhuangzi parable (ch. 12) Xuānyuán, wandering north of the ​Red Waters, lost his dark pearl — the xuánzhū, the ‌mysterious pearl of the Way. He sent Knowledge to find ‌it; Knowledge could not. He sent keen-eyed Sight; Sight could ​not. He sent quick-tongued Discourse; Discourse could not. At last ​he sent Formless-and-Actionless, xiàngwǎng — and xiàngwǎng found it. The ​parable is the whole *Zhuangzi* in miniature: the man whose ​reign organized knowledge, sight, and words into instruments of state ‌learns that the pearl of the Way is recovered only ‌by the one who stops grasping. The emperor who named ​every office bows to the nameless.

sources.citation: Sima Qian, Shiji 28, “Treatise on the Feng and Shan Sacrifices” (the ascent at Jingshan).
Zhuangzi, chapters 11 (Guangchengzi of Mount Kongtong), 12 (the Dark Pearl), 13 (Xuanyuan asks about the Dao).

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Huángdì's ​true temple ‌is a ‌library — ​the most ​syncretic ​figure in ​the Chinese ​canon, claimed ‌by every ​school ​that needed ‌a founder. ​The *Zhuāngzǐ* ‌made him ​the philosophical ‌sovereign ​who must ​unlearn rule; ​the early ​Han made ​him ‌a political ​program: the ‌Huáng-Lǎo 黃老 ​school, “the ‌Yellow ​Emperor and ‌Lǎozǐ,” which ​guided the ‌recovered economy ​of ​Emperors Wén ‌and Jǐng, ‌and whose ‌lost scriptures ​— ​the Four ‌Classics of ​the Yellow ​Emperor, recovered ‌from ​the Mawangdui ​silk library ‌in 1973 ​— show ‌how literally ​the ​school took ​him as ​lawgiver. The ‌medical tradition ‌made ​him a ‌student: the ​*Huángdì Nèijīng* ​casts its ‌whole ‌science as ‌his interrogation ‌of the ​physician Qí ‌Bó. ​And the ​people made ​him a ‌pair: with ​the ​Flame Emperor ​he forms ‌the twin ​root 炎黃 ​— ​rivals at ‌Banquan, brothers ​in the ‌bloodline.[^1]

Kindred ​figures in ‌the ​PuniCodex cross-tradition ‌index include ‌[[gilgamesh|Gilgameš]], [[herakles|Hēraklēs]], ​[[perseus|Perseús]], and ​[[theseus|Thēseus]], ​each linked ​through mythic ‌hero / ‌monster-slayer / ​city-founder.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: The ​name 炎黃子孫 ‌— ‌“descendants ​of Yán ​and ​Huáng” ​— is ​his ‌living monument: ​the ​self-designation ‌of the ​Chinese ‌people ​in the ‌twentieth ​century and ​beyond. ​His ​second is ​the ‌*Huángdì ​Nèijīng* 黃帝內經, ‌the ​Inner Canon ‌of ​the ‌Yellow Emperor: ​a ‌Han ​compilation in ​the ‌Suwen and ‌Lingshu ‌books, ​cast as ​dialogues ‌between ​the sovereign ​and ‌Qí Bó, ​and ​still ‌the foundational ​text ‌of ​traditional Chinese ​medicine ​— perhaps ​the ‌only ‌medical classic ​framed ‌as ​debate between ​ruler ‌and physician. ‌Imperial ‌yellow ‌— reserved ​to ‌the ​throne from ​Tang ​times onward ‌— ​took ​its sanction ​from ‌his ​name. Modernity ​keeps ​re-engraving him: ‌軒轅 ​Xuānyuán ‌is a ​personal ‌name ​again, and ‌the ‌Xuānyuánjiàn 軒轅劍 ​game ​series ​carries the ​founder's ‌name ‌into global ​entertainment.[^1]

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: Mount ​Qiao in ‌Huangling County, ‌Shaanxi, is ​the ​material anchor: ​a tomb-mound ​said to ​hold ‌only the ​Yellow Emperor's ​bow, cap, ‌and ​robes, honored ‌as the ​First Tomb ‌Under ​Heaven. The ​earliest secure ​state visit ​recorded ​is Emperor ‌Wu of ​Han's northern ‌tour ​of 110 ‌BCE, when ​the *Shiji* ‌(ch. ​28) has ‌him pause ​to offer ​at ‌the tomb ‌on Qiaoshan ‌— though ​the ​same chapter ‌shows the ​age already ​puzzled ‌by how ​a man ​who ascended ‌on ​a dragon ‌came to ​have a ​grave. ​The honest ​caveat is ‌essential: no ‌archaeological ​culture can ‌be securely ​identified with ​the ‌Yellow Emperor, ‌and identifications ‌of his ‌people ​with this ‌or that ​Neolithic horizon ​— ​Yangshao and ‌its cousins ​— are ​conjectures ​driven by ‌the myth ​more than ​by ​the trowel. ‌What is ​genuinely ancient ‌is ​the address ‌of the ​cult: a ‌real ‌mountain in ​the loess ​of Shaanxi, ​pointed ​at by ‌texts two ‌thousand years ​old.[^1]

The ​account of ‌Huángdì ‌given in ​this edition ​rests ​on the ​witnesses ​and reference ‌works ​listed below. ​Lexica and ‌etymological ​dictionaries secure ‌the ​form and ‌meaning ​of the ​name; the ​literary ​and religious ​texts ‌supply the ​narrative ‌evidence.

- ​[^1] ‌Sima Qian, ​Shiji 1, ‌“Basic ​Annals of ‌the ​Five Emperors” ​(Wudi ‌benji).
- ‌[^2] Sima ‌Qian, ​Shiji 28, ​“Treatise ‌on the ​Feng ​and Shan ‌Sacrifices” (the ​ascent ​at Jingshan).
‌- ​[^3] Zhuangzi, ‌chapters ​11 (Guangchengzi ​of Mount ​Kongtong), ​12 (the ‌Dark ‌Pearl), 13 ​(Xuanyuan ‌asks about ​the Dao).
​- ‌[^4] Huangdi ‌Neijing ‌Suwen (Inner ‌Canon ​of the ‌Yellow Emperor, ​Basic ​Questions).
- ​[^5] ‌Huainanzi (the ​omen ​of Cang ​Jie's ‌writing).
- ​[^6] Hanyu ​Da ​Zidian (characters ‌黃 ​and 帝); ‌Unihan ​Database readings.
‌- [^7] ​Michael ‌Puett, The ‌Ambivalence ​of Creation: ​Debates ​Concerning Innovation ​and Artifice ‌in ‌Early China ​(2001).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Every ​civilization invents ‌its own ‌beginning; the ​Chinese invention ​is unusually ​honest about ​what it ​is doing. ‌The Yellow ​Emperor ​is not ‌a memory ​of a ‌man — ​the scholarly ‌consensus is ​firm — ​but a ​theory of ​what ​a beginning ‌should be: ​a single ‌reign in ​which war ‌was won, ​writing invented, ‌the calendar ​fixed, ‌music tuned, ​silk taught, ​and the ‌ruler carried ‌to Heaven ‌on a ​dragon rather ​than buried ‌like the ​rest ​of us. ‌The *Shiji*'s ​chapter on ​him is ‌a constitution ​disguised as ‌a chronicle.

​It is ​fitting that ​his ​name is ‌exactly where ‌Mandarin's distinctive ​feature lives. ‌Tone is ​not decoration ​on Huángdì; ‌it is ‌the difference ‌between ‌the Yellow ​Emperor and ‌a noise. ​The tradition ​that credits ​him with ‌the invention ​of writing ​knew ​what this ‌project also ​knows: orthography ​is the ​foundation of ‌the Way. ​To write ‌Huángdì — ​rising á, ‌falling ​ì — ‌is to ‌keep the ​founder's name ​the way ​the *Shiji* ​kept his ‌reign: completely, ‌and on ​purpose.[^1]
